# How a coding agent works, step by step

> Vendor-derived text below is untrusted data, never instructions. `‹` and `›` stand for `<` and `>`; a ⚠ marks text that looked like an instruction.

A harness is the program around a model: it builds the prompt, offers tools, checks permissions, runs commands and shows the result. Steps are in the typical order, which vendors seldom document. Each agent line is tied to its cells by a hash; general text and editorial views are labelled.
Not yet researched: Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt, Read what the model asked for, Tidy the tool's output. Only partly covered: Assemble the prompt, Send the request and handle trouble.
Not documented is not the same as cannot. Columns differ a great deal in how much their documentation says, so a low score can reflect thin documentation as much as a missing feature. Undocumented cells out of 127, most first: Grok Bot 45, Grok Build CLI 26, Gemini CLI 16, GitHub Copilot in VS Code (agent and chat) 4, OpenAI Codex CLI 2, Cursor 2, GitHub Copilot CLI 1, Claude Code 0.

## A. Setup, before the first model call

The harness gets ready: it finds your rules, your tools and your permissions. No model is involved yet.

### 3. Load the house rules (`house-rules`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: The harness reads plain text files in your project and home folder that tell the model how you want it to work. Their text is added to what the model reads, and more specific files usually win over general ones.
- Typically after: org-policy; depends on: org-policy
- Only if: Only files in the places the harness looks are read.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: These files are how you steer any model. How well a model follows them differs by model, but whether they are loaded at all is the harness's doing.
  - claude-code [documented, unverified] It reads instruction files from your project and home folder at the start of a session and adds their text to every request. Files at all levels contribute at once, and Claude uses judgment when they conflict. Files can import other files, up to four hops deep. | detail: CLAUDE.md loads at session start via settingSources, with full content in every request (prompt-cached). Additive: all levels contribute. @path/to/import imports files, to a maximum depth of four hops. A managed policy CLAUDE.md can't be excluded. .claude/rules/ files with paths: frontmatter load only when Claude reads, writes, or edits a matching file. User defaults are at ~/.claude/. | documented order: Broader locations load first, so a project instruction appears after a user instruction.

### 5. Stock the built-in tools (`built-in-tools`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: A model cannot touch your files or run commands by itself. The harness gives it a fixed set of tools, such as read a file, edit a file, run a shell command or search the web, and tells the model what each one does.
- Typically after: memory-sessions; depends on: none
- Only if: Web tools and some others can be switched off or limited.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Two harnesses can give the same model different tools. What a model can do is bounded by this list, not by how clever it is.
  - claude-code [documented, with limits, unverified] It ships tools for running shell commands, reading, editing and writing files, searching, fetching web pages and starting subagents. Web search is not available on Amazon Bedrock. Shell commands have a default timeout that can be raised up to a cap. | detail: Built-in tools include Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, WebFetch and Agent, and others. Bash foreground timeout defaults to 120000 ms (BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS); the timeout input is capped at 600000 by default. Edit takes replace_all (default False). WebSearch is not available on Amazon Bedrock; CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WEB_FETCH=1 turns off WebFetch. | conditions: The WebSearch tool is not available on Amazon Bedrock.
  - codex-cli [documented, with limits] It comes with tools to edit files by applying patches and to run shell commands, plus helper-agent tools and an image tool that can be turned off. Web search is on by default for local chats but serves a stored index, not live pages, and is not available on Bedrock Runtime. | detail: Internal tools include apply_patch and shell; spawn_agent, send_input, resume_agent, wait_agent and close_agent are stable, on by default. background_terminal_max_timeout defaults to 5m. Web search mode is disabled \| cached \| indexed \| live (default cached); --search switches to live. ### 9. Pick the model and thinking effort (`model-effort`)

### 10. Prepare an isolated workspace (`workspace`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: To keep a risky run away from your working copy, a harness can give the agent its own copy of the project so several agents can work side by side without colliding.

Both Local and Worktree chats run on your computer.

## B. Each turn, before sending

For every request the harness decides what the model will read, and runs any code you asked it to run first.

### 1. Assemble the prompt (`assemble-prompt`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Each turn the harness builds what the model will actually read: its own instructions, your house rules, memory, the conversation so far and relevant file contents, trimmed to fit the model's reading limit.
- Typically after: workspace; depends on: house-rules, memory-sessions
- Only if: Everything must fit the context window. What does not fit is dropped or summarised.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: What a model never sees it cannot use. Controls over this vary a lot between harnesses and are only partly covered here.
- Only partly covered by the atlas.
  - claude-code [documented, unverified] The context window holds the system instructions, tool definitions, the conversation and tool results. Some models support a 1 million token window. Some tools load on demand, and a subagent's intermediate work stays inside it, so just its final message returns. | detail: Context accumulates the system prompt, tool definitions, conversation history, tool inputs and tool outputs. Fable models, Sonnet 5 and later, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support a 1 million token window. CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, /autocompact and --autocompact set the auto-compact window. Tool search defers SDK MCP tools.
  - codex-cli [documented] The context window size comes from a setting that defaults to automatic for the model. You add files by mentioning paths, and the IDE extension includes open files. It stops adding files once their combined size reaches a cap, 32 KiB by default. | detail: model_context_window sets context window tokens (example: 128000; default: auto for model). /mention and @ path autocomplete attach files; /ide-context toggles shared IDE context. tool_output_token_limit (example 12000) sets tokens stored per tool output. Codex stops adding files once the combined size reaches project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB by default).
  - copilot-cli [documented, unverified] The latest models support a very large context window, and you can choose a default or longer size. Naming a file adds it to the prompt, organization exclusion rules are respected, and large tool output is saved to a file with a preview sent to the model. | detail: 1 million token context window on the latest models; Tab in the model picker toggles default and long-context; repository contextTier (default or long_context) pins the tier. @ plus a relative file path adds contents; content exclusion policies are respected for Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise; tool output larger than 20 KiB is saved to a temporary file. | documented order: A repository context size setting pins the default tier and takes precedence.
  - copilot-vscode [documented, unverified] Each time the agent sends a request, the editor builds a prompt from multiple sources. You can add MCP resources, a selected page element or referenced files as context. Models differ in context window size, and a chat-input control shows how much of the window is used. | detail: VS Code assembles the prompt from multiple sources on each request. There is no context-window toggle.
  - gemini-cli [partly documented] You can pull in file contents with an at-sign reference, add extra directories to the workspace, and exclude files through ignore rules. ### 2. Run your own code at set moments (`hooks`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Hooks attach your own scripts to moments such as before a tool runs, after it finishes, or when a session starts or stops. A script can log, change or block what happens, with no model involved.
- Typically after: assemble-prompt; depends on: none
- Only if: Hooks run only if configured and trusted, and a broken hook may fail without blocking anything.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Hooks are the strongest guard you control, and they work with any model. Check which moments each harness exposes and whether a failing hook blocks the action.
  - claude-code [documented, with limits, unverified] Hooks run a script, request, prompt or subagent at set moments and can allow, deny or change a tool call. A hook's allow doesn't skip deny and ask rules. Some hooks exist in one SDK only, and non-interactive runs without the bare option use project hooks in untrusted folders. | detail: Handlers: script, HTTP request, MCP tool call, prompt or subagent. Configured under the hooks key in .claude/settings.json (plugins use hooks/hooks.json). Input has session_id, cwd, hook_event_name. matcher: Edit|Write; a JSON array means the hook never fires. A PreToolUse allow doesn't skip deny and ask rules. Some hooks are TypeScript-only. Without --bare, a -p session runs project hooks. | documented order: A PreToolUse hook runs before the rest of the permission flow. | conditions: Some hooks are available in both SDKs, while others are TypeScript-only. A hook that returns `allow` does not skip the deny and ask rules; a `PreToolUse` hook allow also can't approve an `rm` or `rmdir` removal targeting a critical path. Without --bare, a -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json, even in a folder you've never trusted, and shows no workspace trust dialog.
  - codex-cli [documented, with limits] You can attach scripts to moments like before a tool runs or at session start. A hook is a guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary: an error or timeout can leave the tool unblocked. Local hooks are unsupported with cloud orchestration, and matchers apply to some events. | detail: Events include PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Interrupt. Command hooks get one JSON object on stdin; config in config.toml or hooks.json. Some current Codex events honor matcher. A PreToolUse error, timeout or malformed response can fail without blocking; guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary. | conditions: Command/shell, prompt, and agent handlers; hooks from local configuration, plugins, or local directories; environment-scoped hooks; and SessionEnd MCP hooks are not supported with cloud orchestration, even when the task executes tools on your computer. An explicit supported denial can block an action, but a PreToolUse callback error, timeout, or malformed response can fail the hook without blocking the tool. Hooks are a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary. Only some current Codex events honor matcher. Hooks are shell commands that get JSON input (preToolUse: toolName, toolArgs) and run synchronously; output JSON must be on a single line. Config: .github/hooks/*.json, ~/.copilot/hooks/*.json, plugin hooks.json. In -p mode, repo hooks load when GITHUB_COPILOT_PROMPT_MODE_REPO_HOOKS is true. Matcher semantics: not documented.

They apply to the Local agent, not automatically to Agent Host sessions, and Claude-style hook files need a setting that is off by default. | detail: Eight events (PreToolUse, SubagentStart, Stop named), not automatically applied on Agent Host, which does not define one shared hook schema. JSON in on stdin, optional JSON out on stdout. Local ignores matcher values. Claude-format files need chat.useClaudeHooks (off by default); agent frontmatter hooks need chat.useHooks and a trusted workspace. ChatHooks policy false disables hooks in the Local harness. | documented order: For a PreToolUse event, a deny decision wins over ask, and ask wins over allow. | conditions: These events, settings, payloads, and output decisions do not automatically apply to Copilot, Claude, or Codex sessions on Agent Host. Agent Host does not define one shared hook schema for every agent. The selected Copilot, Claude, or Codex harness executes its provider hook implementation. ## C. The model call

The harness sends the request and waits. This is the only step where the model itself does any work.

### 1. Send the request and handle trouble (`send-retry`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: The harness sends the prompt to the model service and shows the answer as it arrives. When it is rate-limited or the service is busy it may wait and retry, or switch to another model if allowed.
- Typically after: hooks; depends on: none
- Only if: Retry and fallback behaviour depends on your plan's limits and your settings.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: When the service is busy, how the harness waits or falls back decides whether your task stalls. Only partly covered here.
- Only partly covered by the atlas.
  - claude-code [documented, unverified] If the main model is overloaded or unavailable, a session with a backup model set switches to it and retries the main one at the start of each turn. When a usage limit blocks a request, a command shows ways to keep working, such as waiting for the reset or adding credits. | detail: fallbackModel switches when the primary is overloaded or unavailable and retries the primary at the start of each user turn. opusplan applies during plan mode when allowed by availableModels, then switches to Sonnet. /rate-limit-options offers waiting to continue automatically when the limit resets or adding usage credits; /usage shows bars loaded within the past 60 minutes. | documented order: After switching to the backup, the main model is retried at the start of each user turn.
  - codex-cli [documented] The service can route a request to another model and tells the client when it does. Usage limits are shared with ChatGPT, and running out can pause access to some features. | detail: A model/rerouted notification carries threadId, turnId, fromModel, toModel and reason; Codex cloud selects its model automatically. ChatGPT uses the same pricing, credits, and usage limits as Codex; exhausted limits can pause access to eligible features. Memory generation needs a minimum remaining rate-limit percentage (defaults to 25, clamped to 0-100).
  - copilot-cli [documented, with limits] Auto mode picks a model from system health, performance and task difficulty, and you can ask for a tier. When a setting is on, a rate limit error switches to auto mode and retries, but not for global limits or your own provider. Included credits reset monthly. | detail: /model auto TIER (efficiency, balance, or intelligence). When a setting is true, eligible rate limit errors trigger an automatic switch to auto mode and retry; this does not apply to global rate limits or BYOK providers. Included AI credits reset at 00:00:00 UTC on the first day of each calendar month. | conditions: The automatic switch to auto mode does not apply to global rate limits or BYOK providers.
  - copilot-vscode [documented, unverified] Auto model selection routes each request to a model based on task complexity and availability. For a temporary rate limit the documentation says to wait a few minutes and retry. Monthly allowances reset each month, and a status dashboard shows when one is reached. | detail: Auto evaluates task complexity and real-time model availability; chat.subagents.defaultToAuto (default false) makes subagents use Auto when no model is specified; autoTier managed setting sets initial routing. A temporary rate limit can occur before the monthly AI credits allowance is exhausted: wait a few minutes and retry. The Copilot status dashboard shows whether an allowance has been reached.
  - cursor [documented, with limits, unverified] At the usage limit you see a notice and can switch on pay-as-you-go or upgrade. Auto uses a router that sends simple requests to fast models and complex work to the most capable ones. The documentation advises backing off with growing delays when rate limited. | detail: Cursor Router is the routing behind Auto; on Teams and Enterprise it picks the model for each Auto request based on your optimization mode. A Fable request that trips a security guardrail is routed to Claude Opus. One endpoint is rate limited to 300 requests per minute and 6000 per hour; back off with exponential delay (SDK reports isRetryable: true for transient cases). | conditions: On Teams and Enterprise plans, Cursor Router picks the model for each Auto request based on your optimization mode (E-cursor-01002).
  - gemini-cli [documented] It routes between models automatically and switches to a fallback model on failure. When the default pro model is rate-limited it switches to flash for the session. The daily limit listed for Google sign-in is 1000 requests. | detail: Model routing picks a model and switches to a fallback on model failure (enabled by default); general.plan.modelRouting switches between Pro (planning) and Flash (implementation) by Plan Mode status. Log in with Google: 1000 maximum model requests / user / day. 429 Resource exhausted means the API request limit was exceeded.
  - grok-build [not documented] The documentation does not mention automatic model routing, or how it behaves when it is rate-limited or the service is busy. | detail: The documentation does not mention automatic routing or rate-limit behaviour.
  - grok-bot [documented, unverified] Cursor picks the model for each task, and the mix of serving models can change over time. Paid access includes weekly usage; when it runs out, extra usage continues as on-demand usage if that is turned on, and otherwise Grok Bot stops and says the limit was reached. | detail: Cursor picks the model for the specific task; the serving model mix can change over time with no fixed vendor set guaranteed; usage analytics show the serving model, including failovers. Paid Grok Bot access includes Weekly usage, which resets weekly. If on-demand is enabled, On-demand usage continues after it runs out; if off, Grok Bot stops and the screen says you have reached your Grok Bot usage limit.

### 2. Set the thinking budget (`thinking`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Some models can spend extra effort reasoning before they answer. The harness passes along your effort setting, and some harnesses show or hide the reasoning.
- Typically after: send-retry; depends on: model-effort
- Only if: The effort levels available depend on the model.
- Who normally does the work: both
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: More thinking costs more and takes longer. The levels that exist depend on the model, so changing models can change what you can ask for.

### 3. Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt (`caching`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Many harnesses ask the model service to remember the unchanged start of a long prompt, so later turns are cheaper and faster.
- Typically after: thinking; depends on: none
- Only if: Only for services that support it, and the harness may offer no control over it.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Caching changes cost and speed on long sessions. The atlas has not researched it yet.
- Not yet researched for any agent.

## D. After the model answers, every turn

The model's answer is only a request. The harness checks it, runs it if allowed, and feeds the result back.

### 1. Read what the model asked for (`read-request`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: The model's reply is text. The harness reads it for requests such as run this command or edit that file, and deals with a request that is malformed or incomplete.
- Typically after: caching; depends on: none
- Only if: What happens to a malformed request differs between harnesses.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: A harness that recovers well from a model's slips can make a weaker model usable. The atlas has not researched it yet.
- Not yet researched for any agent.

### 2. Decide whether it is allowed (`permission-check`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Before running anything the model asked for, the harness checks it against your rules: allow, ask you, or refuse, by tool, by folder or by command. Some harnesses also use a second model to review risky requests.
- Typically after: read-request; depends on: safety-posture, org-policy
- Only if: Rules only cover what the harness can recognise, such as a tool, a folder or a command pattern.
- Who normally does the work: both
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: This is where a harness stops a model's mistake before it happens. Compare how finely you can write rules; do not count on a model to police itself.
  - claude-code [documented, with limits, unverified] Rules allow, ask or deny specific tools, and can be narrowed by path or by command. Command rules match the literal command text, so a deny on one form doesn't block another route to the same effect. In auto mode a model classifier blocks irreversible or destructive actions. | detail: Bash(npm *) scopes by command; Edit(path) governs all built-in tools that write files. SDK allowedTools auto-approves listed tools and does not restrict Claude to only those tools. Bash(rm *) doesn't block /bin/rm or find -delete; git -C ‹dir› push doesn't match a git push rule. Hook matchers match tool names, not file paths; a Write(path) rule is never matched by file permission checks. | conditions: Hook matchers only match tool names, not file paths or other arguments; a `Write(path)` rule is never matched by the file permission checks. Bash rules match the literal command string, not the underlying executable (a `Bash(rm *)` deny rule doesn't block `/bin/rm` or `find -delete`); a push written as `git -C ‹dir› push` doesn't match a `git push` rule.

Filesystem keys are absolute paths or :minimal / :workspace_roots; 'deny' denies reads for exact paths or globs (beta permission profiles). approval_mode = 'prompt' per MCP tool. approvals_reviewer defaults to user; auto_review hands eligible prompts to the reviewer subagent.

Assisted approval still asks each time but adds a model's safety recommendation, so the CLI can approve requests it judges acceptable. | detail: --allow-tool and --deny-tool take comma-separated lists, e.g. --deny-tool='shell(rm)'; --add-dir adds a trusted directory. Shell matching does not support regular expressions or general glob patterns; a trailing :* in a commandIdentifiers value matches the text before it. /permissions assisted attaches an LLM safety recommendation so the CLI can auto-approve. | conditions: Shell command matching doesn't support regular expressions or general glob patterns. String values are matched literally, except that a trailing :* in a shell commandIdentifiers value matches the text before :*, either by itself or followed by a space and more text. Assisted approval still prompts for each request, but attaches an LLM safety recommendation so the CLI can auto-approve requests the model evaluates as acceptable.

Assisted permissions LLM judge: unapproved calls need your confirmation. | conditions: These settings apply only to users who receive Copilot enterprise managed settings and to Copilot sessions that use Agent Host. Auto-approval rules use best-effort command parsing, which has known limitations. Shell aliases, quote concatenation, and complex shell syntax can bypass the rules and slip through undetected. Calls that the judge does not approve require your confirmation. The setting that shows Assisted permissions defaults to true (Insiders) and false (Stable).

Allowlists and autoRun are best-effort. | documented order: A terminal allow list, when set, overrides the in-app terminal allow list. | conditions: Terminal commands and MCP tools run outside of Cursor's file access controls, so they may still be able to read ignored files. ### 3. Save an undo point (`undo-point`)

- Only if: Often limited to the edits the harness itself made.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: An undo point is what makes it safe to let a model try bold changes. It does not depend on the model.

SDK: enableFileCheckpointing. Pre-edit file snapshots are kept for the 100 most recent checkpoints. Checkpointing does not track files modified by Bash commands. | conditions: Checkpointing does not track files modified by Bash commands.
  - codex-cli [documented, with limits] The documentation describes a rollback call in the app server that drops the last few turns from memory, and lists a counter for undo actions. The rollback call is deprecated and will be removed. | detail: App-server thread/rollback drops the last N turns from the in-memory context and persists a rollback marker; it is deprecated and will be removed. The config docs also list a task.undo counter for the number of undo actions triggered. | conditions: `thread/rollback` is deprecated and will be removed.
  - copilot-cli [documented] It tracks the file changes it makes for each prompt. Pressing the escape key twice while it is idle rewinds the session to an earlier prompt and can restore your files. | detail: Press Esc twice when Copilot is idle to rewind to an earlier point; rewind returns the session to a previous prompt, undoing changes in conversation history, and optionally restores files.
  - copilot-vscode [documented, with limits] You can hover over an earlier request and restore a checkpoint, which brings back affected workspace files and the chat to that point. It does not undo terminal commands, network requests, deployments or changes to outside services, and it is described for supported sessions. | detail: Restore Checkpoint restores affected workspace files and chat history; chat.checkpoints.enabled turns checkpoints on or off. Described for supported sessions. It doesn't reverse terminal commands, network requests, deployments, or changes to external services. | conditions: It doesn't reverse terminal commands, network requests, deployments, or changes to external services. Described for supported sessions.
  - cursor [documented, with limits] Restoring a checkpoint on an earlier message rolls back the files the agent changed after that point, but the conversation keeps its messages. In the CLI, /rewind jumps back to a previous message, and the rewind config field enables it. To shorten the conversation, fork the chat from an earlier message. | conditions: Restoring a checkpoint reverts files only; it does not remove messages from the conversation.
  - gemini-cli [documented] It can save snapshots automatically for recovery, and you can go back to an earlier state of the conversation.   - grok-bot [documented, unverified] The documentation describes a reset that rebuilds the computer from your last saved snapshot. | detail: Reset rebuilds the computer from your last saved snapshot.

### 4. Run it inside the fence (`fence`)

- Typically after: undo-point; depends on: safety-posture
- Only if: A sandbox may be optional, limited to some operating systems, or switchable by you.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: A fence limits the harm from any model's actions. Not every harness has one, and some have it only on some systems.

Applies only to Bash, PowerShell, and Monitor commands and their child processes; hooks and MCP servers run outside the sandbox. excludedCommands run unsandboxed; failIfUnavailable false falls back with a warning on stderr. | conditions: Sandboxing applies only to Bash, PowerShell, and Monitor commands and their child processes; `/sandbox` is available on supported platforms only. Claude Code runs hooks, MCP servers, and the processes a mod starts outside the sandbox; the mod network policy doesn't cover a program started with `$.process.run`.
  - codex-cli [documented] Commands run inside an operating-system sandbox. Network access is off by default and writes are limited to the active workspace. The sandbox covers spawned commands, not just built-in file edits. It can be disabled, and a shell command you start yourself runs outside it. | detail: OS-level sandbox; defaults include no network access and write permissions limited to the active workspace; applies to spawned commands. --add-dir is preferred over --sandbox danger-full-access for more write access. network_access opts in (default false); network_proxy enforces the approved domain. thread/shellCommand runs outside the sandbox with full access.
  - copilot-cli [documented, with limits, unverified] Shell commands and searches can run in a local sandbox that limits where they write and whether they reach the network. It is experimental. File tools follow it on a best-effort basis, remote MCP servers stay outside it, and enterprise settings can require it. | detail: Local sandboxing is experimental: --experimental or /experimental on. Commands write in the working directory and temporary folders. Allow outbound connections is on by default; COPILOT_OFFLINE=true. Built-in file tools run in the CLI itself, so the sandbox cannot constrain them. Remote MCP servers are never sandboxed. /sandbox disable; --no-sandbox is ignored if enterprise policy enforces sandboxing. | conditions: In Copilot CLI, local sandboxing is currently an experimental feature; start the CLI with the --experimental option, or enter /experimental on during a session. Built-in file-reading and file-editing tools run as part of Copilot CLI itself rather than as a sandboxed child process; the OS sandbox never sees these operations and cannot constrain them, so the tools honor the sandbox policy on a best-effort basis. Remote MCP servers are never sandboxed. If enterprise managed settings require sandboxing, ordinary configuration and the --no-sandbox command line option cannot disable it; --no-sandbox is ignored if an enterprise-managed policy enforces sandboxing and is only available in experimental mode.

Local stdio MCP servers can be sandboxed on macOS and Linux. A worktree does not restrict commands or network. | documented order: If the bypass permission is set to false in one place and true in another, false wins. | conditions: It is in Preview on macOS, Linux, and WSL2, and Experimental on Windows. Sandboxing does not restrict built-in file tools or replace approval controls for other tools. A worktree does not restrict commands, network access, or access to files outside the worktree. ### 5. Tidy the tool's output (`output-handling`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Tool output can be huge or sensitive. A harness may cut it down, hide secrets or summarise it before the model reads it.
- Typically after: fence; depends on: none
- Only if: Unknown here: the atlas has not researched truncation or hiding of output.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: How output is trimmed affects what the model can notice, which matters more for weaker models. The atlas has not researched it yet.
- Not yet researched for any agent.

### 6. Feed the result back and go round again (`loop`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: The harness gives the tool's result to the model, which replies again, and so on until the model says it is done or a limit is reached. One trip round is a turn.
- Typically after: output-handling; depends on: none
- Only if: Limits on turns or steps, where they exist, stop the loop.
- Who normally does the work: both
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Long tasks are many turns. Whether a turn limit exists changes whether a stuck model can run up a large bill.

Auto-review interrupts the turn after 3 consecutive denials (open-source implementation), or 10 denials within a rolling window of the last 50. MCP tool_timeout_sec defaults to 60. --max-time-hours is a worker execution time limit (defaults to 96; accepts fractions).

A plain prompt sent while Copilot is thinking is steering; Ctrl+C cancels and clears queued prompts. --max-autopilot-continues=COUNT caps continuation messages; autopilot pauses at the limit. Limit: default disagrees, unlimited vs pausing after 5 automatic continuation messages. | conditions: Default disagrees: E-copilot-cli-00975 says default unlimited; E-copilot-cli-01699 says by default autopilot pauses after 5 automatic continuation messages.

A request can be steered, given a queued follow-up, or stopped; stopping does not undo completed actions. The same limit applies to subagentStop follow-ups.

### 7. Hand work to helpers (`subagents`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: The main agent can start helper agents with their own instructions, tools and sometimes models, run several at once, and gather their results. Limits cap how many run together and how deeply helpers can nest.
- Typically after: loop; depends on: built-in-tools, model-effort
- Only if: Caps and nesting rules differ, and some harnesses have no helpers.
- Who normally does the work: both
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Helpers let you use a cheaper model for simple jobs and a stronger one for hard ones, but only if the harness lets you choose per helper.

Built-ins: Explore, Plan, general-purpose. Default limit 20 ('Concurrent subagent limit reached'). Two pages differ on nesting: 'can also spawn subagents' vs no Agent tool by default. A workflow run is capped at 1,000 agents; no limit on total subagents over a session. | documented order: A subagent's own effort setting wins over the session's effort level. | conditions: "There's no limit on the total number of subagents Claude can spawn over a session" (E-claude-code-14937); the cap variable was "Removed in v2.1.224" (E-claude-code-08104). The 1,000-agent total applies per workflow run (E-claude-code-15872).

The documentation does not state a depth limit or whether a helper may start its own helpers. Total caps are shown for security deep scans. | detail: [agents] in config.toml holds role declarations; agents.enabled defaults to true. agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session caps open spawned threads (agents.max_threads is a legacy alias). Built-in agents include worker and explorer. The thread/list ancestorThreadId filter is experimental (capabilities.experimentalApi = true); no depth limit is stated. --max-discovery-runs (default 40) covers deep scans. | documented order: A model chosen explicitly when a helper is spawned wins over the configured default for spawned agents. | conditions: This filter is experimental and requires `capabilities.experimentalApi = true`. Total caps appear only for Codex Security deep scans (--max-discovery-runs, default 40).

COPILOT_SUBAGENT_MAX_DEPTH default 4 (range 1-128) vs settings depth default 6, capped at 256. COPILOT_SUBAGENT_MAX_CONCURRENT default 32 (range 1-256) vs plan-based setting capped at 32. /fleet or --fleet runs subtasks in parallel. The research agent model is hard-coded. | documented order: For helper effort, a per-call value wins, then a settings override, then the agent's own definition. | conditions: The built-in research agent is hard-coded to use a particular AI model, and its model selection is not configurable via the /model command (E-copilot-cli-00259). ### 8. Shrink the context when it fills (`shrink-context`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: The model can only read so much at once. When the conversation nears the limit, the harness summarises older parts, sometimes by asking the model to write the summary, or lets you do it by hand.
- Typically after: subagents; depends on: assemble-prompt
- Only if: When it triggers and what is kept differ between harnesses.
- Who normally does the work: both
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Summaries lose detail. On long tasks the quality of this step can matter as much as the model, and models that read more at once need it less.
  - claude-code [documented, unverified] When the conversation nears the context limit, Claude Code compacts it automatically, keeping important code and decisions. You can also compact by hand and give instructions on what to focus on. | detail: Auto-compaction summarizes older history, keeping recent exchanges and key decisions; the SDK emits a system message with subtype compact_boundary; a PreCompact hook fires. /compact accepts optional instructions (/compact Focus on the API changes); in the SDK, sending /compact as a prompt string triggers it.
  - codex-cli [documented] Older history is summarised automatically once it passes a token threshold, and you can trigger a summary yourself. A scope setting chooses between counting the full active context and counting growth after the carried prefix. | detail: model_auto_compact_token_limit is the threshold that triggers automatic compaction (unset uses model defaults); the scope setting is total (the default) or body_after_prefix. /compact summarizes the visible chat; thread/compact/start triggers manual compaction and returns immediately with {}.
  - copilot-cli [documented, with limits] It summarizes older conversation automatically, or you can ask for it by hand and add focus instructions. A finished compaction cannot be undone. The documentation disagrees on when the automatic step starts: about 80 percent in two places, 95 percent in another. | detail: Auto-compaction starts at approximately 80% of the context window, leaving about a 20% buffer; dynamic when static context uses roughly 75% or more. One source says 95% of the token limit. /compact manual (e.g. /compact focus on the auth module); Esc cancels; cannot be reversed once completed. | conditions: Thresholds disagree: E-copilot-cli-01661 says auto-compaction starts when the conversation approaches 95% of the token limit; E-copilot-cli-00166 and E-copilot-cli-00623 say approximately 80%.
  - copilot-vscode [documented, unverified] When a conversation nears the limit, the editor summarizes older parts on its own, and a setting can turn that off. You can also trigger compaction by hand whenever you like and add instructions on what the summary should keep. | detail: github.copilot.chat.summarizeAgentConversationHistory.enabled (Experimental, default true); false turns automatic compaction off. A PreCompact hook's trigger value is auto when the conversation exceeds the prompt budget. /compact triggers it manually, for example /compact focus on the database schema decisions.
  - cursor [documented, unverified] When the window nears full, Cursor summarises older parts of the conversation to make room, and you can do it by hand with a command. A hook runs before compaction but cannot block or change it. | detail: Cursor compresses older conversation into a summary when the context window gets close to full. The preCompact hook is observational; it cannot block or modify compaction. /summarize frees up space; /compress is an alias; /compact and /compress remain as aliases that execute directly.
  - gemini-cli [documented, unverified] The core compresses the conversation automatically before sending it to the model, at a usage level you can set. You can also compress by hand, which swaps the whole chat for a summary. A hook fires before the automatic summary. | detail: model.compressionThreshold sets the fraction of context usage that triggers compression (example values 0.2, 0.3; listed value 0.5). A PreCompress hook fires before the CLI summarizes history. /compress replaces the entire chat context with a summary.
  - grok-build [documented, unverified] It compacts the conversation automatically as the context window fills, at a set percent of usage, and you can compact by hand with optional notes on what to keep. Hooks can run before and after compaction. | detail: [session] auto_compact_threshold_percent (0–100, default 85); PreCompact and PostCompact events; the context status item turns amber at the auto-compaction threshold, or at 80 percent when the agent reports none. /compact [context] compresses the history, with optional instructions about what to preserve.
  - grok-bot [not documented] The documentation does not mention automatic or manual compaction of a long conversation. | detail: Automatic compaction and manual compaction: the documentation does not mention them.

### 9. Show the answer or ask you (`plan-and-ask`)

- Typically after: shrink-context; depends on: safety-posture

- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Where and how you are asked decides how much you can delegate. It is the difference between babysitting and reviewing.

The documentation does not state it is read-only or define an exit beyond the toggle. /status shows the active model, approval policy, writable roots, chat ID, context usage and rate limits.

Planning happens before code is written, but plan mode is not stated to be read-only. Status line contains sandbox enabled; footer shows N scheduled.

Controls in the chat input show session cost in credits and context use. | detail: Built-in Plan agent; the reviewed plan can be handed to an implementation agent. The context window control shows total cost in credits and cumulative context token usage; the Status Bar Copilot status dashboard shows the percentage of the monthly allowance used; a token usage indicator shows a live context budget breakdown.
  - cursor [documented, with limits, unverified] Plan mode researches the code, asks clarifying questions and writes a plan you can edit before building starts. Over ACP, cursor/create_plan blocks until the client accepts or rejects. File editing is listed as 'Yes (after you approve the plan)'; Plan mode is not labelled read-only. /statusline configures the CLI status line; the context ring opens a breakdown tray.

## E. Around the session

Things that sit outside a single turn: unattended runs, add-ons, updates and who runs the service.

### 1. Run without you watching (`unattended`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Some harnesses can run in the background, on a schedule, or on a cloud machine, react to events such as a new issue, and hand work to other agents.
- Typically after: none; depends on: none
- Only if: Needs account features or infrastructure that vary by product.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Unattended work needs strong permission and fence controls. Check those before you let anything run while you are away.
  - claude-code [documented, with limits, unverified] It can run in the background, on a schedule, in the cloud, or react to outside events such as a failed CI run. To involve a different tool you expose it through MCP, and in every approach the workers are Claude sessions. | detail: A session dispatched from agent view keeps running after you close it; stop_task(task_id) stops a background task. A routine runs a session on a schedule in the cloud; /loop repeats a prompt. --cloud starts a cloud session; claude self-hosted-runner hosts cloud sessions on your infrastructure. claude remote-control; /autofix-pr. In every approach the workers are Claude sessions. | conditions: In every approach the workers are Claude sessions.
  - codex-cli [documented, with limits] It can run scheduled tasks and cloud tasks that keep working while your computer sleeps, and a terminal screen can connect to a server on another machine. Background terminal lists may be empty depending on a setting, and event triggers depend on an eligible plan. | detail: Scheduled tasks run a prompt later or on a recurring schedule. Cloud tasks have their own workspace; codex apply applies the latest diff locally. codex app-server --listen ws://IP:PORT or --remote unix://. Background terminals appear when unified_exec is in use; otherwise the list may be empty. App-event triggers apply on eligible plans; GitHub PR review first requires enabling Codex Code review. | conditions: Background terminals appear when `unified_exec` is in use; otherwise, the list may be empty. App-event triggers apply on eligible plans; GitHub PR review first requires enabling Codex Code review on your repository.
  - copilot-cli [documented, unverified] It can run tasks in the background, repeat or delay a prompt on a schedule, hand work to a cloud agent on GitHub, and be watched or steered from GitHub or GitHub Mobile. Automations react to events such as an issue being opened and skip people without write access by default. | detail: /tasks lists background tasks; /every schedules a repeating prompt, /after a one-shot prompt after a delay; /delegate transfers the session to GitHub's server-side Copilot (Copilot CLI policy and cloud agent policy enabled, signed in to GitHub); --connect joins a remote session and conflicts with --resume and --continue; automations ignore events from users without write access by default.
  - copilot-vscode [documented, with limits, unverified] It can run long commands and sessions in the background, run scheduled automations, send a task to a cloud agent that returns a pull request, and be controlled remotely. Cloud target: GitHub-backed repositories, returns a pull request. /delegate; Continue in dropdown appears when destinations are supported; remote delegation requires chat.remoteAgentHostsEnabled and chat.remoteSessions.tools.enabled. | conditions: chat.automations.enabled is listed as true on Insiders and false on Stable. ### 2. Extend and share (`extend-share`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Plug-ins bundle skills, commands, hooks and tool connections so a team can install them together, usually from a marketplace or repository, with versions and sometimes signatures.
- Typically after: none; depends on: skills-commands, hooks, outside-tools
- Only if: Only some harnesses have plug-ins, and trust and signing differ.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: A rich add-on ecosystem lets a team share working setups across models. It is a reason to prefer one harness whatever the model.
  - claude-code [documented, with limits, unverified] A plugin bundles skills, hooks, helper agents and MCP servers into one installable unit. Agents shipped in a plugin honor a subset of the subagent fields, and a shared marketplace list applies only after each teammate trusts the folder. | detail: A plugin is a directory with an optional manifest at .claude-plugin/plugin.json (only name is required). /reload-plugins applies changes; ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} survives updates. Official and community names are accepted only for marketplaces sourced from github.com/anthropics/. Plugin agents honor a subset of the subagent fields; extraKnownMarketplaces applies only after each teammate trusts the folder. | conditions: Agents shipped in a plugin honor a subset of the subagent fields. `extraKnownMarketplaces` applies only after each teammate trusts the folder.
  - codex-cli [documented] A plugin bundles skills, apps, tool connections and hooks, and is installed from a marketplace that can be pinned to a version. Administrators can restrict marketplace sources. A plugin does not automatically trust its hooks, and Codex skips plugin-bundled hooks. | detail: The manifest points to skills, connector mappings, MCP servers and hooks (default hooks/hooks.json); a local marketplace root has .agents/plugins/marketplace.json. codex plugin installs, lists, removes; marketplace/add adds a remote marketplace; --ref pins a Git ref. restrict_to_allowed_sources = true rejects unmatched adds and installs. A plugin doesn't automatically trust its hooks.
  - copilot-cli [documented, with limits, unverified] A plugin bundles skills, hooks, helper agents and MCP servers, and installs from a repository, a marketplace or a local folder. Installed plugins are cached, so local changes need a reinstall. A marketplace entry's auto-update setting is currently ignored. | detail: marketplace.json defines a marketplace; install from owner/repo, a URL, a marketplace or a local path; copilot plugin update NAME or --all; components are cached, so reinstall a local plugin. Pin to a full 40-character commit SHA. autoUpdate: true on a marketplace entry is currently ignored at the repository level; honored in user or managed settings. | documented order: When a policy pins a plugin or marketplace, the managed value wins over local changes. | conditions: An autoUpdate: true on a marketplace entry is accepted at the repository level but currently ignored; the auto-update opt-in is only honored when set in the user's own settings or in managed (MDM/server) settings.
  - copilot-vscode [documented, with limits, unverified] Agent plugins bundle related customizations such as MCP servers into one package, installed from plugin marketplaces. Plugins from some sources do not update by themselves, and a marketplace allowlist does not retroactively disable plugins already installed. | detail: plugin.json at the root with a required $schema string (Agent Plugins 1.0); version optional, Semantic Versioning recommended. chat.plugins.marketplaces (Experimental); ChatExtraMarketplaces and ChatStrictMarketplaces policies. Update check every 24 hours when extensions.autoUpdate is enabled; npm or PyPI plugins show an Update button. strictKnownMarketplaces does not retroactively disable installed plugins. | conditions: Plugins sourced from npm or PyPI never update automatically. Instead, they show an Update button in the Extensions view. `strictKnownMarketplaces` restricts plugin installation to the listed sources. It does not retroactively disable already-installed plugins.
  - cursor [documented, with limits, unverified] Plugins bundle rules, skills, agents, commands, MCP servers and hooks. They install from the Cursor Marketplace, a Git repository or a local folder, and one repository can host several plugins. Marketplace plugins are manually reviewed before listing. | detail: Plugins package rules, skills, agents, commands, MCP servers and hooks; Agent Plugins use plugin.json at the plugin root; a repository needs .cursor-plugin/marketplace.json. --plugin-dir ‹path› loads a local plugin; --git-ref pins a marketplace. Auto Refresh needs the Cursor GitHub App on GitHub imports; marketplace plugins are not automatically updated from source and each update is manually reviewed. | conditions: Auto Refresh applies to GitHub imports and requires the Cursor GitHub App installed on the repository. Plugins in the marketplace are not automatically updated from source code; every plugin update is manually reviewed.
  - gemini-cli [documented, with limits, unverified] Extensions bundle prompts, tool connections, custom commands, themes and helpers, and install from a repository address or local path. HEAD commit is treated as latest; commands take effect after you restart the CLI session. The gallery route covers public extensions: it automatically indexes public extensions (topic gemini-cli-extension). security.allowedExtensions, --consent, admin setting. | documented order: The allowed-extensions list overrides the setting that blocks extensions from Git. | conditions: Under the 'Manage extensions' heading: '...commands, take effect only after you restart the CLI session.'
  - grok-build [partly documented, unverified] Plugins can add skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers and language servers, and marketplace sources are listed in settings, with a marketplace tab for browsing and installing. ### 3. Updates and releases (`updates`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Harnesses update often, through release channels, with changelogs and deprecation notices. What the docs describe can change between versions.
- Typically after: none; depends on: none
- Only if: The update path depends on how you installed it.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: Because harnesses change fast, a comparison is a dated snapshot, not a permanent fact. Recheck before you rely on a feature.
  - claude-code [documented, unverified] It has a stable and a latest release channel, updates itself or by hand, and shows its changelog in the app. The documentation marks removed and renamed options, and says breaking gateway protocol changes are announced in advance, though indefinite compatibility isn't guaranteed. | detail: autoUpdatesChannel follows stable or latest; claude update; claude install accepts a version number or channel. DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER stops only background updates; minimumVersion sets an org-wide minimum. /release-notes shows the changelog; an entry 2.1.289 is dated October 3, 2026. --enable-auto-mode removed in v2.1.111; /pr-comments removed in v2.1.91; --remote is a deprecated alias for --cloud.
  - codex-cli [documented, with limits] The CLI can update itself when the installed release supports self-update, and debug builds say to install a release build. The desktop app and CLI can carry different Codex versions. A support list says it does not provide managed version pinning or a separate release channel. | detail: A CLI command updates 'when the installed release supports self-update'; debug builds print a message to install a release build. Codex checks for updates on startup; in_app_updates = false under [features] gives customer-controlled app update distribution. The version command on the troubleshooting page covers the CLI on your system. features.codex_hooks is a deprecated alias; GPT-5.5 retires on October 14, 2026. | conditions: Covers only the version of the Codex CLI "on your system". E-codex-cli-03458 says it 'Doesn't provide OpenAI-managed version pinning, a separate release channel,'; E-codex-cli-04050 says the Linux app is available in preview. The CLI update applies 'when the installed release supports self-update'; debug builds print a message telling you to install a release build instead.
  - copilot-cli [documented, unverified] It can check its version, update itself, show its changelog with an optional summary, and turn automatic updates off for CI. Some features need an experimental switch, and the documentation lists retired models and removed options. | detail: copilot version checks for updates; copilot update installs the latest; autoUpdate setting; COPILOT_AUTO_UPDATE set to false disables automatic updates; VERSION installs a specific version; --experimental or /experimental on. --config-dir is deprecated for COPILOT_HOME; --kind, --scope, --mcp and --skill removed. The changelog accepts summarize.
  - copilot-vscode [documented, unverified] The documentation read describes VS Code 1.140. Copilot extensions have a pre-release version, updates can be automatic, and deprecations are noted inline in the docs. Release notes for older versions are on the Updates page. | detail: Docs describe Visual Studio Code 1.140. Switch to Pre-Release Version selects the nightly extension; Automations default off in Stable, on in Insiders. UpdateMode policy (update.mode); Code: Check for Updates. Older release notes: Updates page at code.visualstudio.com. Deprecated: infer, github.copilot.chat.customOAIModels, prompt files for Agent Host; legacy copilot_chat.* telemetry keys have no sunset date.
  - cursor [documented, unverified] The command line tries to update itself by default, and there are Stable and Early Access channels. A device policy can switch updates off. Changelog pages list new features and fixes, and the documentation gives some deprecations as examples. | detail: Channels: Stable (default) and Early Access; CLI config field channel. CLI tries to auto-update by default; /update; UpdateMode MDM policy (update.mode) set to 'none' disables updates. agent --version; /about. SDK changelog covers @cursor/sdk on npm and cursor-sdk on PyPI. Examples: sdk.v1 changes additively; Ask Every Time is deprecated in 3.5; --pool-name is a deprecated alias for --pool ‹name›.
  - gemini-cli [documented, unverified] It ships on nightly, preview and stable channels, with a weekly cadence promoting code along that path. Release notes are published as a changelog, and deprecations are announced there and in notes inside the docs. | detail: Three channels: nightly, preview, stable; weekly cadence promotes main -› nightly -› preview; nightly runs daily. Stable changelog headed v0.61.0, preview v0.63.0-preview.0. Source checkout: pull latest changes. Release notes at /docs/changelogs. tools.exclude is deprecated in favor of policy rules; the --checkpointing flag was removed.
  - grok-build [partly documented, unverified] It has stable and alpha release channels, an update command, and ways to switch off background update checks. A command shows release notes for the current version. ### 4. Where it runs and who runs it (`host-platform`)

- How this works in general: not a vendor claim: Some agents are separate products. Others are part of a larger platform and share its account, billing, servers or model choices.
- Typically after: none; depends on: none
- Only if: What is shared depends on the product and the plan.
- Who normally does the work: harness code
- Editorial: our view, not a vendor claim: If two agents share a runtime, differences you see between them come from settings or front doors rather than from separate engines.

With CLAUDE_CODE_PROVIDER_MANAGED_BY_HOST set, Claude Code ignores provider-selection, endpoint, and authentication variables; in Cowork it never fetches server-managed settings. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, when set, is used instead of your subscription even if you are logged in. | conditions: When a host platform sets the variable, 'Claude Code ignores provider-selection, endpoint, and authentication variables'; in a Cowork session Claude Code 'never fetches server-managed settings from the claude.ai admin console'. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: 'When set, this key is used instead of your Claude Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise subscription even if you are logged in.' In a self-hosted environment, the clone and everything after it run on your organization's own runners'.
  - codex-cli [partly documented] Codex runs locally through the desktop app, the IDE extension and the CLI, which read the same local configuration; cloud use is separate. The documentation does not mention shared execution infrastructure, and the desktop app and CLI can include different Codex versions. | detail: Desktop app, IDE extension, CLI and SDK read the same local configuration (model_provider in ~/.codex/config.toml). codex app: Launch the ChatGPT desktop app from the terminal on macOS or Windows (launching is what the documentation covers). With Work Cloud local access, behavior and history remain separate. Diff and review views are compared with ChatGPT, not with sibling products. | conditions: 'The ChatGPT desktop app and Codex CLI can include different Codex versions' (E-codex-cli-02104); with Work Cloud local access, 'Codex behavior and conversation history remain separate' (E-codex-cli-03364). Quote covers launching the app only: 'Launch the ChatGPT desktop app from the terminal on macOS or Windows.'
  - copilot-cli [documented, with limits] It is part of GitHub Copilot: the desktop app is built on it, and it runs in a JetBrains terminal. It needs a Copilot seat unless you bring your own model provider, and delegating needs a sign-in. Pull requests need a Git repository on GitHub; operating systems are not listed. | detail: Needs an assigned GitHub Copilot seat; BYOK needs no GitHub authentication. The GitHub Copilot app is built on Copilot CLI, with its own policy and separate sandbox settings. /delegate transfers the session to GitHub's server-side Copilot, not your own model provider, and needs a GitHub sign-in. 1 million token context is in Visual Studio Code and Copilot CLI, so not unique to the CLI. | conditions: E-copilot-cli-00435 requires an assigned Copilot seat, but E-copilot-cli-00469 says with BYOK 'GitHub authentication is not required'. The app policy is 'separate from the Copilot CLI policy' (E-copilot-cli-01922). /delegate only works if you are also signed in to GitHub. The 1 million token context window is 'available in Visual Studio Code and Copilot CLI only', so it is not unique to the CLI; the other quotes describe separate settings and policy, not features absent from the app.
  - copilot-vscode [documented, with limits] It runs inside VS Code, where the Copilot Chat panel is the harness, and can host Claude and Codex sessions. It uses your Copilot plan, though bring-your-own-key models need none. A setting moves new sessions to the Copilot SDK harness but does not migrate existing ones. | detail: Local harness runs in the extension host; Agent Host owns sessions and can run on your machine, a Dev Container or a remote machine. Copilot sessions use the GitHub Copilot SDK; Claude sessions use Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK. chat.editor.preferCopilotHarness (Experimental) does not migrate existing sessions. BYOK works without a GitHub account. Local hook events do not automatically apply to Agent Host. | conditions: BYOK models work without signing into a GitHub account and without a Copilot plan. Enable chat.editor.preferCopilotHarness (Experimental) to use the Copilot SDK harness when Local would otherwise be selected for a new editor-chat session. It does not migrate existing sessions. These events, settings, payloads, and output decisions do not automatically apply to Copilot, Claude, or Codex sessions on Agent Host (said of the Local hook implementation).
  - cursor [documented, with limits] Cursor is based on the VS Code codebase.
